desc:
You are building n towers in a row. Tower i may have any integer height h[i] with 1 ≤ h[i] ≤ maxHeights[i]. The heights must form a mountain: there is a peak index k such that h is non-decreasing up to k (h[0] ≤ h[1] ≤ ... ≤ h[k]) and non-increasing after it (h[k] ≥ h[k+1] ≥ ... ≥ h[n-1]).

Return the largest possible value of h[0] + h[1] + ... + h[n-1].

Example: maxHeights = [5, 3, 4, 1, 1] gives 13 with heights [5, 3, 3, 1, 1] (peak at index 0). With [6, 5, 3, 9, 2, 7] the answer is 22, using [3, 3, 3, 9, 2, 2].
hints: Try every index as the peak. For a fixed peak, each tower should be as tall as the limits allow. How tall can tower k - 1 be, and tower k - 2?
With peak k at its own limit, tower j < k gets min(maxHeights[j..k]), and symmetrically on the right. Summing this for every peak directly is O(n2) or worse; reuse work between peaks.

Let left[i] be the best sum of towers 0..i when tower i is the peak. Find the nearest index j < i with a smaller limit using a stack: left[i] = left[j] + maxHeights[i] * (i - j). Do the mirror image for right, and combine at each peak.
editorial: Fix the peak i and give it height maxHeights[i]. Raising the peak never hurts, since all other heights are only capped from above by the minimum limit between them and the peak. For towers on the left, h[j] = min(maxHeights[j..i]).

Let j be the nearest index left of i with maxHeights[j] < maxHeights[i] (or -1). Towers j+1..i all get exactly maxHeights[i], because everything between is at least as high. Towers at or before j are capped by the minimum up to j, which is the same situation as peak j. So left[i] = left[j] + maxHeights[i] * (i - j) with left[-1] = 0. The index j comes from a monotonic stack. The right side right[i] is the mirror image.

The total for peak i is left[i] + right[i] - maxHeights[i] (the peak is counted twice) and the answer is the maximum over all i. Time O(n), space O(n). The maximum sum is below 5 * 108, within 32 bits.
